Sixth-generation (6G) wireless networks are expected to provide ubiquitous
connectivity for a massive number of Internet-of-Things (IoT) devices
\cite{cai2026,xu2026}. To serve devices in remote areas with limited terrestrial
coverage, low Earth orbit (LEO) satellites complement cellular networks for
applications such as smart agriculture and climate monitoring \cite{shen2025}. These
power-limited devices transmit short packets sporadically, with only a small
fraction active at a given time \cite{shen2025,cai2026}. In grant-based random
access, handshaking before transmission incurs significant
signaling overhead, while the long propagation delay of terrestrial-satellite links
further increases access latency \cite{cai2026,xu2026}. Accordingly, grant-free
random access (GFRA) allows active devices to transmit pilots and data directly
without first obtaining a grant, reducing signaling overhead and access latency in LEO satellite IoT
systems \cite{cai2026,xu2026}.

Supporting GFRA over LEO links requires handling large delays and Doppler shifts
caused by long propagation distances and high satellite mobility. The 3rd Generation
Partnership Project (3GPP) Release 17 framework addresses these effects through
device-side precompensation assisted by the global navigation satellite system
(GNSS) \cite{3gpp38300}. With such precompensation, many existing satellite GFRA
schemes assume perfect compensation or small residual delays and Doppler shifts at
the receiver \cite{shen2025}. However, frequent estimation and compensation increase
energy consumption and reduce battery lifetime, making these schemes less suitable
for power-limited remote IoT devices \cite{shen2025}. This motivates reducing
dependence on GNSS, consistent with the GNSS-independent operation considered in the
Release 19 study on satellite access \cite{3gpp22865}. With reduced reliance on
device-side precompensation, the satellite receiver must accommodate
large differential delays and Doppler shifts, which can cause severe inter-symbol
and inter-carrier interference in conventional orthogonal frequency division
multiplexing (OFDM) systems \cite{shen2025,huang2026}.

To mitigate these effects, orthogonal time frequency space (OTFS) modulation
exploits the quasi-static properties of channels in the delay--Doppler domain
\cite{shen2025,hadani2017}. In \cite{shen2025}, multi-frame OTFS transmission
handles large differential delays and Doppler shifts at the satellite receiver,
allowing devices to operate without GNSS assistance or precompensation of these
offsets. However, the two-dimensional transformation in OTFS entails relatively high
modulation complexity \cite{ding2026,huang2026}. Affine frequency division
multiplexing (AFDM), based on one-dimensional chirp modulation, offers lower
modulation complexity than OTFS while retaining strong Doppler robustness over
doubly dispersive channels \cite{bemani2022,ding2026,huang2026}. With properly
designed chirp parameters, AFDM can also achieve full diversity over such channels
\cite{bemani2022}. This combination of low modulation complexity and full diversity
makes AFDM attractive for GFRA with power-limited IoT devices.

To unleash the full potential of AFDM-GFRA, accurate joint activity detection and
channel estimation (JADCE) is a critical prerequisite \cite{ding2026}. Existing
methods exploit sporadic device activity to formulate JADCE as a compressed sensing
(CS) problem and incorporate structured priors to capture channel sparsity
\cite{shen2025,ding2026}. The scheme in \cite{ding2026} further uses a graph neural
network to adaptively learn sparsity patterns, while retaining a predefined
delay--Doppler grid for the sparse channel representation. However, in practical
propagation environments, fractional Doppler shifts and fractional time delays can
introduce significant power leakage in the effective channel matrix, thereby
weakening its sparsity \cite{huang2026}. This motivates learning effective-channel
priors from data to capture channel structures beyond the assumed sparse
representation \cite{cai2026,huang2026}.

Score-based generative models learn channel priors from samples by estimating the
score function of the channel distribution \cite{song2019,arvinte2023}. In
\cite{huang2026}, score-based learning is performed directly on the AFDM effective
channel to address fractional delay--Doppler off-grid leakage in channel estimation.
For massive random access, \cite{ying2026} proposes a two-stage algorithm that first
identifies active devices through a Transformer-based detector and then uses
generative diffusion models for joint channel estimation and data detection.
However, both approaches rely on iterative posterior sampling, which requires
repeated score function evaluations and incurs substantial computational cost
\cite{huang2026,ying2026}.

To avoid iterative posterior sampling, \cite{cai2026} develops a score-based turbo
message passing (STMP) algorithm that incorporates generative channel priors for
JADCE. Through Tweedie's formulas, separate first- and second-order score networks provide
posterior means and variances for single-step minimum mean-squared error (MMSE)
denoising under equivalent additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) observations.
However, this AWGN model is justified in the large-system
limit with right-rotationally invariant random sensing matrices \cite{cai2026}.
In the finite-dimensional, structured multi-frame AFDM system considered here,
departures from these conditions can exacerbate the mismatch between denoiser
input errors and the white Gaussian perturbations used for training. A similar
limitation has been highlighted for structured compression matrices in \cite{wei2026}. This
mismatch can degrade channel denoising accuracy and, consequently, JADCE
performance. Moreover, \cite{cai2026} computes activity probabilities using
Gaussian extrinsic messages obtained after projecting the channel posterior onto
a Gaussian distribution. In general, matching posterior means and variances does
not preserve the marginal likelihood associated with a non-Gaussian channel
prior. Consequently, the resulting likelihood ratio can yield inaccurate
activity probabilities even when the channel posterior moments are accurately
estimated. These errors further affect the activity-weighted channel estimates
exchanged with the linear estimation module.

Against this background, we investigate GNSS-independent AFDM-GFRA for
LEO satellite IoT systems. Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

\begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*)]
\item We develop a multi-frame AFDM transmission scheme that handles large differential
delays and Doppler shifts at the satellite receiver. The derived input--output
relationship retains fractional delay--Doppler effects and the chirp-periodic prefix
phase for delays exceeding the useful symbol duration. Separating the phase
evolution across frames yields a multiple measurement vector (MMV) model in which
the effective channel of each device remains approximately constant over
consecutive frames. Additional pilot frames therefore provide more observations
without increasing the number of channel coefficients to be estimated.

\item We learn a score-based generative prior directly from multiantenna AFDM
effective-channel samples with fractional delays and Doppler shifts.
The denoiser is trained using colored Gaussian perturbations, and the learned
prior provides channel posterior mean and variance estimates for message passing.

\item We develop a message-passing JADCE receiver for the structured multi-frame AFDM
observation model. A learned density-ratio estimator compares the active and inactive
observation distributions under the effective-channel prior to obtain soft activity
probabilities. These probabilities are combined with channel posterior mean and
variance estimates obtained using the learned prior to form Gaussian extrinsic
messages for iterative exchange with the linear estimation module.
Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed receiver improves activity
detection and channel estimation performance compared with STMP across different
signal-to-noise ratios and pilot-frame counts.
\end{enumerate}

Sixth-generation (6G) networks must connect large numbers of
Internet-of-Things (IoT) devices, including remote, power-limited
devices served by low Earth orbit (LEO) satellites
\cite{cai2026,xu2026,shen2025}. Their short, sporadic transmissions
favor grant-free random access (GFRA), which avoids the handshaking
overhead and propagation latency of grant-based access
\cite{cai2026,xu2026}.

LEO links introduce large delays and Doppler shifts. The 3rd Generation
Partnership Project (3GPP) Release 17 framework uses global navigation
satellite system (GNSS)-assisted device-side precompensation
\cite{3gpp38300}; many satellite GFRA schemes consequently assume
perfect compensation or small residual offsets \cite{shen2025}.
Frequent estimation and compensation consume energy, motivating
GNSS-independent operation as considered in the Release 19 study
\cite{3gpp22865}. The receiver must then accommodate large differential
delays and Doppler shifts, which cause inter-symbol and inter-carrier
interference in orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM)
\cite{shen2025,huang2026}.

Orthogonal time frequency space (OTFS) modulation exploits quasi-static
delay--Doppler channels \cite{shen2025,hadani2017}. Multi-frame OTFS
in \cite{shen2025} handles these offsets without device-side GNSS
precompensation, but its two-dimensional transformation incurs higher
modulation complexity \cite{ding2026,huang2026}. Affine frequency
division multiplexing (AFDM) uses one-dimensional chirp modulation
and, with suitable chirp parameters, achieves full diversity over
doubly dispersive channels at lower modulation complexity
\cite{bemani2022,ding2026,huang2026}.

AFDM-GFRA requires joint activity detection and channel estimation
(JADCE). Compressed sensing (CS) methods exploit sporadic activity
and structured channel sparsity \cite{shen2025,ding2026}; the graph
neural network in \cite{ding2026} learns sparsity patterns on a
predefined delay--Doppler grid. Fractional delays and Doppler shifts,
however, cause power leakage that weakens effective-channel sparsity
\cite{huang2026}, motivating priors learned directly from channel
samples \cite{cai2026,huang2026}.

Score-based generative models learn such priors through the channel
distribution's score function \cite{song2019,arvinte2023}.
The AFDM estimator in \cite{huang2026} addresses fractional
delay--Doppler leakage, while \cite{ying2026} combines a Transformer
activity detector with diffusion-based channel estimation and data
detection. Both require repeated score evaluations for iterative
posterior sampling. Score-based turbo message passing (STMP)
\cite{cai2026} instead uses Tweedie's formulas and separate first-
and second-order score networks for single-step minimum mean-squared
error (MMSE) denoising under equivalent additive white Gaussian noise
(AWGN) observations.

The AWGN approximation is justified in the large-system limit with
right-rotationally invariant sensing matrices \cite{cai2026}.
Finite-dimensional, structured multi-frame AFDM can depart from these
conditions, increasing the mismatch between denoiser input errors and
white-noise training perturbations; a related limitation is reported
in \cite{wei2026}. Furthermore, STMP computes activity probabilities
from Gaussian extrinsic messages after posterior projection.
For a non-Gaussian channel prior, matching posterior moments need not
preserve the marginal likelihood. The resulting activity-probability
errors can therefore affect channel estimation even when the
conditional moments are accurate.

We investigate GNSS-independent AFDM-GFRA with the following contributions:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*)]
\item A multi-frame AFDM model retains fractional delay--Doppler effects
and CPP phases for delays exceeding the useful symbol duration.
Separating inter-frame phases yields a multiple measurement vector
(MMV) model: additional pilot frames provide observations of the
same effective channel without increasing its dimension.
\item A score-based generative prior is learned from multiantenna AFDM
effective channels using colored Gaussian perturbations. The trained
denoiser provides posterior means and variances for message passing.
\item A learned density-ratio estimator supplies soft activity
probabilities, which combine with the channel moments to form
Gaussian extrinsic messages. The resulting JADCE receiver improves
on STMP across the evaluated SNR and pilot-frame grids.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Receiver Structure}
\label{sec:receiver-structure}

The factorization in \eqref{eq:working-posterior} separates the
multi-frame observation likelihood from the channel and activity
priors. Following the turbo message-passing structure in
\cite{ma2015,cai2026}, we organize the receiver into two modules:
multi-frame linear estimation (MFLE) and generative-prior-aided joint
denoising (GPJD), as illustrated in Fig.~\ref{fig:receiver-structure}.
The modules exchange Gaussian extrinsic messages parameterized by
a mean and a scalar variance, with $\widehat{\mathbf A}$ and
$\widehat\sigma^2$ fixed within the transmission block.
